performers: Soojin Han, violin; Hankyung Arte Philharmonic; Seokwon Hong, conductor
question: What changes when the soloist opens the concerto?
intro: The soloist enters at once, without the usual orchestral exposition, and the cadenza arrives before the recapitulation. Follow the E minor theme, the tranquil G major second theme, a cadenza written out by the composer, and a recapitulation that begins over the soloist’s arpeggios. All three movements of this set come from one live concert.

cues.title: The soloist enters at once
cues.text: There is no orchestral exposition: the solo violin plays the E minor theme almost immediately, over murmuring strings, held notes in the clarinets and bassoons, and plucked basses. Mendelssohn had told his friend David that this theme “gives me no peace”.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia describes the almost immediate violin entry; the score (printed p. 1) shows the violin entering in the second bar over strings, held clarinet and bassoon notes and pizzicato basses. The key estimate is E minor (0.74–0.85) at 0:00–0:25 and the level rises from −24.4 dB at 0:00 to −16.7 dB at 0:05.

cues.title: Running notes take over
cues.text: From about 0:25 the violin’s line fills with continuous running notes, and the detected note onsets rise from under one to three or four a second. The theme gives way to virtuoso passage-work while the strings keep a steady pulse beneath.
cues.evidence: The detected onset density rises from 0.8 per second at 0:20 to 2.4 at 0:25, 3.4 at 0:35 and 3.6 at 0:40. Detected onsets are not note counts; the score (printed pp. 2–3) shows continuous sixteenth-note figuration in the solo part.

cues.title: A rush upward, then the tutti
cues.text: A fast rising run in the violin leads, at about 1:05, to the orchestra’s first tutti: the level rises about eight decibels and the attacks stop as long fortissimo chords sound. The orchestra then restates the opening theme.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −18.2 dB at 1:00 to −10.4 dB at 1:05 and stays near −11 dB at 1:10, with 0.0 detected onsets in both windows. Wikipedia says that after a bravura of rapidly ascending notes the orchestra restates the theme; the score (printed p. 4) shows the ascending run before fortissimo chords.

cues.title: A restless transition
cues.text: From about 1:35 to 2:45 the music alternates swells and falls, with the soloist’s passage-work answered by the orchestra. Wikipedia calls this a frenetic chromatic transition. Listen for the harmony to keep slipping away from E minor.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia describes the frenetic chromatic transition. The level moves between −11.0 dB and −18.6 dB across 1:30–2:40, with detected onsets between 0.6 and 3.2 per second; the report has boundaries at 2:26, 2:32, 2:40 and 2:44. The key estimates move between B minor, A, D and B♭ areas and are not used as chord labels.

cues.title: A concerto “for you”
cues.text: On 30 July 1838 Mendelssohn wrote to Ferdinand David, the Leipzig Gewandhaus concertmaster, that he would like to write him a violin concerto and that one in E minor kept running through his head. It took him another six years to finish.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article on the concerto quotes the letter of 30 July 1838 and gives the six-year delay; the IMSLP work page gives the dedication to David and the composition years 1838–44.

cues.title: A tranquil second theme
cues.text: At about 3:10 the music settles in G major. The woodwinds sing the second theme while the soloist sustains a pedal note on the open G string, and the detected note activity falls to almost nothing.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is G major (0.87–0.88) at 3:15–3:25 with 0.0–0.4 detected onsets per second and the level between −19 and −23 dB; the report has a boundary at 3:08 (0.40). Wikipedia describes woodwinds with a G pedal in the soloist’s part; the score (printed p. 9) is marked “tranq.” and pp.

cues.title: The violin sings it
cues.text: After the woodwinds, the solo violin takes the second theme itself. In this stretch, from about 3:35, the level stays between −17 and −21 dB and the detected attacks arrive about once a second or less, so the melody has the foreground.
cues.evidence: The level is −17.5 dB at 3:35, −20.6 dB at 3:40 and −17.4 dB at 3:50, with 0.2–1.4 detected onsets per second at 3:35–3:55. The Wikipedia article says the soloist plays the tune after the woodwinds.

cues.title: A manuscript found in 1989
cues.text: An autograph of the concerto came to light in 1989 in the Jagiellonian Library in Kraków. It marks the first movement “Allegro con fuoco” — with fire — rather than the printed “Allegro molto appassionato”, and differs in the solo passage-work.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article reports the Kraków manuscript, its tempo marking and the differences in the solo part; which text this performance follows is not documented.

cues.title: The exposition ends on a held chord
cues.text: The exposition closes quietly: the level dips to about −33 dB at 4:25, the lowest value so far, and the score shows a fermata on a chord before the development begins. Wikipedia says a short codetta ends the exposition.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −16.2 dB at 4:15 to −22.2 dB at 4:20 and −32.6 dB at 4:25, then rises to −26.0 dB at 4:30; the report has a boundary at 4:32 (0.50). The score (printed p. 10) shows a fermata chord after a crescendo.

cues.title: The development begins
cues.text: At about 4:32 the development opens quietly and builds. Wikipedia says the two main themes are combined here. The level rises from −26 dB to −13 dB in ten seconds and the detected onsets climb to three or four a second.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −26.0 dB at 4:30 to −18.9 dB at 4:35 and −12.8 dB at 4:40; onsets rise from 1.6 to 4.4 per second by 4:55. The report has a boundary at 4:32 (0.50); the score (printed p. 11) opens softly with pizzicato strings. The combination of the two themes is from Wikipedia.

cues.title: Two themes in one
cues.text: In the development the first theme’s rising energy meets the second theme’s calm. Listen for the singing G-major tune in the woodwinds returning against the violin’s running notes, which are still pressing forward.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia states that the opening two themes are combined in the development; this is a listening suggestion for the whole stretch, not a timed entrance. The level stays between −9.9 and −15.5 dB at 4:45–5:20 with 1.6–4.4 detected onsets per second.

cues.title: The development’s peak
cues.text: From about 5:30 to 5:45 the whole orchestra holds near −10 dB, among the loudest stretches of the development, with the soloist’s figuration running beneath. The local key estimate is A minor.
cues.evidence: The level is −9.2 dB at 5:30, −9.9 dB at 5:35, −11.1 dB at 5:40 and −10.6 dB at 5:45, with 0.6–1.8 detected onsets per second; the local key is A minor (0.66–0.78) at 5:35–5:50, an approximate estimate. The 5:30 window is among the five loudest.

cues.title: Staying near B
cues.text: Between 6:00 and 6:40 the bass moves between B and F♯, and the key estimates favour B minor. Listen for the way the harmony stays close to the dominant of E minor while the surface keeps changing.
cues.evidence: The bass pitch class is B or F♯ at 6:00–6:35 (B at 6:05, 6:15, 6:20 and 6:35; F♯ at 6:00, 6:10 and 6:30); the local-key estimate is B minor (0.74–0.93) at 6:00–6:20. The estimates are approximate and not chord labels.

cues.title: A loud peak before the fade
cues.text: At about 6:30 the orchestra reaches a loud peak, near −10 dB. The sound then begins to fall: by 6:45 the level has dropped by more than ten decibels as the development starts to wind down.
cues.evidence: The level is −10.4 dB at 6:30 and −11.2 dB at 6:35, then −14.8 dB at 6:40 and −22.3 dB at 6:45; the 6:30 window is among the five loudest.

cues.title: A long diminuendo
cues.text: From about 6:45 the music fades towards pianissimo over half a minute: the level falls from −22 dB to −36 dB by 7:10, among the quietest windows of the movement. The score marks “dim.” and “sempre più piano”.
cues.evidence: The level is −22.3 dB at 6:45, −28.9 dB at 6:50, −30.7 dB at 7:00, −33.7 dB at 7:05 and −36.0 dB at 7:10, with 0.0–0.4 detected onsets per second at 6:50–7:10. The 7:05 and 7:10 windows are among the five quietest. The score (printed p. 16) marks “dim.” and “sempre più piano”.

cues.title: The autograph and the premiere
cues.text: Mendelssohn’s autograph is dated 16 September 1844, but he went on asking David for advice. He was too ill to conduct the premiere in Leipzig on 13 March 1845, and Niels Gade conducted it with David as soloist.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article gives the autograph date and the premiere; the IMSLP work page gives the date, the Gewandhaus, David as soloist and Gade as conductor.

cues.title: A crescendo on the dominant
cues.text: At about 7:18, the report’s strongest boundary, the music begins a long crescendo from piano to fortissimo over a held B in the bass, the dominant of E minor. By 7:40 the level reaches one of the loudest windows in the file.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is at 7:18 (novelty 1.00); the level rises from −27.4 dB at 7:15 to −13.3 dB at 7:35 and −9.4 dB at 7:40 (a loudest window), with bass B and a B major key estimate (0.77–0.84) at 7:15–7:40. The score (printed p. 17) marks “poco a poco cresc.” before the cadenza.

cues.title: The cadenza, written out
cues.text: At about 7:42 the orchestra stops and the soloist plays the cadenza alone. Mendelssohn wrote it out in full, instead of leaving it to be improvised, and placed it before the recapitulation, not at the movement’s end.
cues.evidence: The level is −9.4 dB at 7:40 with 0.0 detected onsets (a held chord), then −18.4 dB at 7:45 with 3.0 onsets as the solo passage-work begins; the score (printed p. 17) is headed “Cadenza ad libitum”. Wikipedia describes the written-out cadenza and its position. Which published cadenza this soloist plays is not documented.

cues.title: The cadenza quickens
cues.text: Wikipedia says the cadenza builds speed through quavers, quaver triplets and finally semiquavers, played with ricochet bowing. In this recording the passage-work runs at about two to three detected onsets a second between 7:45 and 8:00.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia describes the rhythmic stages and the ricochet bowing; the detected onsets are 3.0, 2.6, 2.6 and 2.4 per second at 7:45–8:00, which cannot separate the rhythmic stages. The time of each stage is not claimed.

cues.title: The quietest point
cues.text: Around 8:15 the soloist reaches the quietest point in the movement, near −43 dB: a very soft passage inside the cadenza before the sound builds again. Listen for how much room the unaccompanied violin has here.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −23.6 dB at 8:05 to −32.5 dB at 8:10 and −42.9 dB at 8:15, then −36.0 dB at 8:20 and −25.6 dB at 8:25; the 8:15 and 8:20 windows are the two quietest of the file; the report has a boundary at 8:08 (0.40).

cues.title: A bright, soft sound
cues.text: At about 8:50 the sound becomes very bright and very soft: the spectral centroid rises to about 3,560 Hz, the highest in the file, while the level falls to −33 dB. It is consistent with the high ricochet arpeggios in which Wikipedia says the cadenza ends.
cues.evidence: The centroid is 3,557 Hz at 8:50, against 1,900–2,300 Hz in neighbouring windows, with the level at −32.8 dB at 8:50 and −32.7 dB at 8:55 and 0.4 detected onsets per second at 8:50. That this is the ricochet passage is an inference from the sound and Wikipedia’s description.

cues.title: The theme returns over arpeggios
cues.text: At about 9:02 the report finds a boundary: the orchestra takes the opening melody while the soloist’s rippling ricochet arpeggios continue. Wikipedia calls this a novel role for a violin soloist, who here acts as the accompanist. The level dips to −36 dB at 9:15.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 9:02 (0.41); the level is −26.5 dB at 9:00, −20.7 dB at 9:05, −22.2 dB at 9:10 and −36.0 dB at 9:15, before the tutti at 9:25. The theme in the orchestra and the arpeggios are from Wikipedia; the score (printed p. 18) shows soloist arpeggios marked pp.

cues.title: The recapitulation’s tutti
cues.text: Between about 9:15 and 9:25 the level swells from pianissimo, and by 9:25 the full orchestra is back at fortissimo. For half a minute, 9:30–9:55, the level stays between −8.5 and −12.7 dB, the loudest sustained stretch of the movement.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −36.0 dB at 9:15 to −26.0 dB at 9:20 and −13.1 dB at 9:25, then stays between −8.5 and −12.7 dB until 9:55; the 9:35, 9:45 and 9:50 windows are among the five loudest. The key estimate is E minor (0.74–0.83) at 9:30–9:55.

cues.title: Towards E major
cues.text: After the tutti, from about 10:00, the sound softens and the key estimate drifts from E minor to B and then to E major. Listen for the orchestra preparing the second theme’s return, now in the tonic major.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −12.7 dB at 9:55 to −19.1 dB at 10:00 and −26.4 dB at 10:10; the key estimate is B minor (0.73–0.78) at 10:00–10:05, B major (0.76–0.82) at 10:10–10:15 and E major (0.95) at 10:20. The estimates are approximate.

cues.title: The second theme in E major
cues.text: At about 10:20 the second theme returns in E major, the tonic major, in place of the exposition’s G major. For about thirty seconds the key estimate is an almost perfect fit to E major, and the detected note onsets fall to near zero.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is E major at 0.95–0.98 across 10:20–10:40, with 0.0–1.0 detected onsets per second and the level between −18.7 and −23.1 dB; the report has a boundary at 10:22 (0.51). Wikipedia says the second theme is played in E major in the recapitulation.

cues.title: A harmonic detour and a loud close
cues.text: From about 10:50 the key estimates swing towards C♯ and then B. At 11:10 and 11:15 the sound swells again to −14 dB in E major before dropping sharply at 11:20. Listen for the harmony straying and the tonic returning.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is C♯ minor/major (0.75–0.82) at 10:50–11:00, B major (0.67) at 11:05 and E major (0.87–0.93) at 11:10–11:20; the level is −14.4 dB at 11:10 and −14.9 dB at 11:15, then −27.5 dB at 11:20; the report has boundaries at 10:46, 10:56 and 11:10 (0.52). The estimates are approximate.

cues.title: “The heart’s jewel”
cues.text: In 1906 the violinist Joseph Joachim, at his 75th birthday party, called the Germans’ four great violin concertos: Beethoven’s the greatest, Brahms’s equal in seriousness, Bruch’s the richest, and Mendelssohn’s “the most inward, the heart’s jewel”.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article quotes Joachim’s toast as reported in its source; it is a secondary report of a spoken remark.

cues.title: The coda begins
cues.text: At about 11:40 the level rises from −29 dB to −16 dB in five seconds and detected note activity jumps to three or four a second. Wikipedia says the music gathers speed into the coda, which is marked “Presto”.
cues.evidence: The level is −28.8 dB at 11:40, −15.8 dB at 11:45 and −13.9 dB at 11:50, with detected onsets rising from 0.8 to 3.6 per second; the report has a boundary at 11:40 (0.48). The score (printed pp. 24–26) marks “Più presto”, “Sempre più presto” and “Presto”.

cues.title: Faster and faster
cues.text: From about 11:50 to 12:40 the detected onsets stay between about two and three and a half a second while the level holds between −12 and −21 dB. The score asks for “più presto”, then “sempre più presto”, and finally “presto”, so the tempo keeps rising.
cues.evidence: The onsets are 3.6, 3.2, 3.4, 2.2, 2.4, 1.6, 2.6, 3.4, 3.4, 2.4 and 3.0 per second at 11:50–12:40, and the level is between −12.1 and −20.7 dB. The tempo markings are from the score (printed pp. 25–26); this recording’s tempo curve is not measured.

cues.title: The transition recalled
cues.text: Wikipedia says a variant of the first movement’s chromatic transition passage ends the movement. In the last minute the level runs between −9.6 and −18.5 dB and the key estimates alternate between B and E. Listen for the earlier restlessness returning.
cues.evidence: The Wikipedia article describes the variant of the chromatic transition; the level is between −9.6 and −18.5 dB at 13:05–13:45 with 1.0–2.6 detected onsets per second, and the key estimates alternate between B major/minor and E major/minor. No time is claimed for the first bar of the variant.

cues.title: The last chord, and a held note
cues.text: In the closing stretch the file stops on the final chords at about 13:52, with the bass on B. In the score the bassoon keeps that B sounding into the Andante, joining the movements without a break. Wikipedia says the linking was designed to eliminate applause.
cues.evidence: The level is −10.1 dB at 13:40, −10.4 dB at 13:45 and −12.2 dB at 13:50, with the bass on B throughout 13:35–13:50 and 0.0 detected onsets at 13:50; the file ends at 13:52.6. The bassoon note and the purpose of the link are from Wikipedia.

transitions.title: A run upward opens the tutti
transitions.how: The soloist’s theme gives way to rushing passage-work and a fast rising run. At about 1:05 the orchestra enters in a first tutti: the level rises about eight decibels, the attacks stop and long fortissimo chords sound. In a classical concerto the orchestra would have begun the movement; here it takes the theme from the soloist, so the roles are reversed. The orchestra restates the opening melody while the soloist rests, and returns with its own figuration soon after.
transitions.evidence: The level rises from −18.2 dB at 1:00 to −10.4 dB at 1:05 with 0.0 detected onsets at 1:05–1:10. Wikipedia says the orchestra restates the opening theme after a rapid ascent; the score (printed p. 4) shows the ascending run and fortissimo chords.

transitions.title: The restlessness subsides into G major
transitions.how: The chromatic transition runs through swells and falls and subsides from about 2:40; the level drops to −26 dB by 2:55. At about 3:10 the music settles in G major, the relative major of E minor, and the woodwinds take up the second theme while the soloist sustains a pedal on the open G string. The sound changes from restless to tranquil without a pause: the soloist’s motion slows and the woodwinds sing.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −16.5 dB at 2:40 to −26.3 dB at 2:55; the key estimate is G major (0.87–0.88) at 3:15–3:25 with 0.0–0.4 detected onsets per second; the report has boundaries at 2:44 (0.70) and 3:08 (0.40). Wikipedia describes the subsiding transition and the woodwind theme over the soloist’s G pedal.

transitions.title: A fermata, then a hushed development
transitions.how: The exposition ends on a chord with a fermata after a crescendo, and the level dips to about −33 dB at 4:25. The development then begins quietly, with the soloist and pizzicato strings, and builds in energy over the next minute. There is no orchestral announcement, and the rising figure of the first theme and the second theme’s calm are combined, according to Wikipedia. The pause marks the join more clearly than any change of key.
transitions.evidence: The level is −22.2 dB at 4:20, −32.6 dB at 4:25 and −26.0 dB at 4:30, then −12.8 dB at 4:40; the report has a boundary at 4:32 (0.50). The score (printed pp. 10–11) shows a fermata chord and a pianissimo opening to the development with pizzicato strings.

transitions.title: A held B, then the soloist alone
transitions.how: After a long diminuendo, the music grows again over a held B in the bass, the dominant of E minor, from piano to fortissimo. At about 7:40 the orchestra holds a loud chord, with no detected attacks, and the soloist enters alone with the cadenza. Placing the cadenza here, before the recapitulation, makes the dominant chord an expectant pause rather than a final cadence; Mendelssohn wrote the cadenza out in full.
transitions.evidence: The level rises from −27.4 dB at 7:15 to −9.4 dB at 7:40 with bass B and a B major estimate (0.77–0.84), then −18.4 dB at 7:45 with 3.0 detected onsets per second; the report has a boundary at 7:18 (1.00). The score (printed p. 17) marks “poco a poco cresc.” and “Cadenza ad libitum”.

transitions.title: The cadenza’s arpeggios become an accompaniment
transitions.how: The cadenza ends in rippling ricochet arpeggios that do not stop: they continue under the orchestra, which plays the opening melody. At about 9:02 the recapitulation therefore begins without a break, with the soloist as accompanist. The level dips to about −36 dB at 9:15 under the arpeggios before the tutti arrives at 9:25.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 9:02 (0.41); the level is −26.5 dB at 9:00, −20.7 dB at 9:05, −22.2 dB at 9:10 and −36.0 dB at 9:15; the centroid is 3,557 Hz at 8:50. Wikipedia says the cadenza links to the recapitulation, where the orchestra plays the opening melody over the soloist’s continuing ricochet arpeggios; the score (printed p. 18) shows the arpeggios marked pp.

transitions.title: Back to the tranquil theme, in E major
transitions.how: After the tutti of the recapitulation the sound softens and the harmony settles on B, the dominant. At about 10:20 the second theme returns, now in E major, the tonic major, instead of the G major of the exposition: the key estimate fits E major almost perfectly for about half a minute. It is the same tune, but the move to the major of the home key changes its colour, and the detected note activity falls to almost none, as it did in the exposition.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −12.7 dB at 9:55 to −26.4 dB at 10:10; the key estimate is B minor/major (0.73–0.82) at 10:00–10:15 and E major (0.95–0.98) at 10:20–10:40 with 0.0–1.0 detected onsets per second; the report has a boundary at 10:22 (0.51). Wikipedia says the second theme is played in E major.

transitions.title: A hush, then the coda takes off
transitions.how: The recapitulation’s closing group ends in a fall: the level drops to about −33 dB at 11:30–11:35, with the key estimate on F♯ major. At about 11:40 the coda begins and the level jumps from −29 dB to −16 dB, with detected note activity rising from under one to over three a second. The score marks “Più presto”, “Sempre più presto” and “Presto”, so the movement gathers speed to its end.
transitions.evidence: The level is −27.5 dB at 11:20, −33.1 dB at 11:30, −32.4 dB at 11:35, −28.8 dB at 11:40, −15.8 dB at 11:45 and −13.9 dB at 11:50; onsets rise from 0.8 to 3.6 per second; the report has a boundary at 11:40 (0.48). The tempo markings are from the score (printed pp. 25–26).

source.title: Mendelssohn, Violin Concerto in E minor, Op. 64, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel; Rietz edition, Serie 4 No. 18). The text this performance follows is not documented.
source.locator: I. Allegro molto appassionato, printed pp. 1–27. Entries are proportioned between the report’s anchors and approximate; scoring read from the score is limited to the passages named.

timeline.note: The soloist states the theme at once over murmuring strings, held clarinet and bassoon notes and plucked basses.
The orchestra’s first tutti, fortissimo, then the opening theme restated while the soloist rests (printed p. 4).
The second theme: flutes and clarinets sing over the soloist’s held low G, with the orchestral strings resting (printed p. 9).
The soloist takes the second theme, with soft strings returning beneath it.
The development opens softly: the soloist with pizzicato strings.
The development’s peak: the whole orchestra with the soloist’s figuration.
The long diminuendo: soft sustained winds, murmuring strings and the soloist’s arpeggios.
The flutes, oboes and first violins carry the opening melody over the soloist’s pianissimo ricochet arpeggios; clarinets, bassoons, horns and a timpani note join in the second bar (printed p. 18).

The second theme again, now in E major: flutes, oboes, clarinets and bassoons sing over the soloist’s sustained note, with horns joining later in the phrase and the orchestral strings resting (printed p. 20).
The coda: the whole orchestra with the soloist, gathering speed.

fields.note: The video description on the YouTube channel named “한수진 Soojin Han” reads “Vn. Soojin Han / Cond. Seokwon Hong / Orch. Hankyung Arte Philharmonic”. The Commons file page names only the orchestra as author, linking the orchestra’s own site. That site’s news column reports a later concert (September 2026) played by the orchestra under a conductor named 홍석원 (Hong Seok-won, professor at Seoul National University), which supports the association but says nothing about the 2022 concert. No roster of players is given, and no second source for the soloist was opened.

fields.note: Commons records the YouTube address as source, so the file is derived from the video’s audio; the three movement files total 1,734.4 s against 1,809 s for the video, leaving about 75 s unaccounted for (tuning, silence, applause or titles), and the cut points are not documented. The processing history before upload is unknown, and the bit rates are from the Commons media record and ffprobe.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain by age: Mendelssohn died in 1847.
fields.note: The Commons file pages carry no composition notice. The conclusion rests on the composer’s death date, which the IMSLP work page and Wikipedia give; it does not license a modern critical edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 (CC BY 3.0), through the “YouTube CC-BY” licence template on Commons. Rights rule 1: the licence covers the sound recording.
fields.note: The Commons file page applies {{YouTube CC-BY}}, whose text says the video or audio excerpt was released under the Creative Commons option on YouTube before August 2025 (then CC BY 3.0). The licence is set by the YouTube channel, which the Commons page does not name as author; the page shows no LicenseReview mark, and the YouTube page as fetched did not display its licence line, so the YouTube setting itself was not seen. The Commons author link goes to the orchestra’s own site (hkphil.com, titled 한경arte필하모닉), so the named author is the orchestra, but that site does not itself state the licence.

composer.epithet: A composer-conductor who turned quicksilver string writing, Bachian counterpoint and remembered landscapes into tightly organised concert music.
facts: Piano with Ludwig Berger; composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter in Berlin
Music director, Düsseldorf, 1833–35; Gewandhaus conductor, Leipzig, from 1835; founder of Leipzig Conservatoire, 1843
Brother of Fanny Hensel; married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children
Symphonies, concert overtures, concertos, oratorios, chamber music and Songs without Words
composer.background:
Felix Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg in 1809 and grew up in Berlin, where his father Abraham’s banking wealth supported an unusually extensive education. His grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn; Felix and his siblings were baptised as Christians in 1816, and the family used the additional surname Bartholdy. He studied piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter, alongside his elder sister Fanny. The family’s concerts extended their classroom education with repeated opportunities to hear their own music, revise it and discuss it with experienced performers.

Zelter’s teaching joined Bach’s counterpoint to classical forms. The boy wrote string symphonies, concertos and chamber works before the pieces usually treated as his starting point. At sixteen he composed the E♭ major Octet, Op. 20, for four violins, two violas and two cellos. Its eight independent parts create different densities inside one ensemble: the first violin’s long ascent, the other instruments’ pulsing accompaniments and the finale’s fugal entries continually reshape the texture. The scherzo’s soft, rapid articulation became a recurrent technical problem in his later orchestral writing.
